objectives.text: The learner can separate a projectile's motion into independent horizontal and vertical parts
The learner can find the time of flight from the vertical motion alone
The learner can predict how range changes with launch angle

say: Here is the whole idea, and everything else follows from it. A projectile is doing two completely separate things at once. Sideways, nothing pushes it, so it just keeps going. Downwards, gravity pulls on it the whole time. The two do not talk to each other.

board.text: Horizontal: constant velocity. Vertical: constant acceleration, 9.81 metres per second squared, downwards.

question: Before we go on — while the ball is in the air, what is its horizontal acceleration?
options: It depends on the launch angle
It decreases as the ball slows
why: the whole lesson rests on the horizontal and vertical being independent

say: Exactly zero. Nothing pushes it sideways once it has left your hand, so the sideways speed never changes. That is why the time in the air comes entirely from the vertical part.

board.text: System: a ball, treated as a point. Assumptions: no air resistance, flat ground, g constant.

purpose: working out where a ball launched at 20 metres per second at 40 degrees actually lands
source:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

v, theta, g = 20.0, np.radians(40), 9.81
t_flight = 2*v*np.sin(theta)/g
t = np.linspace(0, t_flight, 200)
x = v*np.cos(theta)*t
y = v*np.sin(theta)*t - 0.5*g*t**2

plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.2))
plt.plot(x, y, lw=2)
plt.xlabel('distance (m)'); plt.ylabel('height (m)')
plt.title('20 m/s at 40 degrees')
plt.grid(alpha=0.3)
print(f'time of flight {t_flight:.2f} s, range {x[-1]:.1f} m, peak {y.max():.1f} m')
stdout: time of flight 2.62 s, range 40.2 s, peak 8.4 m

say: Two point six seconds in the air, forty metres down the field, peaking at eight and a half metres. Notice the shape is a perfect parabola — that falls straight out of a linear horizontal motion combined with a quadratic vertical one.

board.caption: 20 metres per second, launched at 40 degrees

board.text: Sanity check: eight metres is about a two-storey house. That is the right sort of size for a hard throw.

say: Now the question people actually care about. What angle throws it furthest? Multiply the time of flight by the horizontal speed and you get the range, and the answer is hiding in a trig identity.

lines.note: using 2 sin θ cos θ = sin 2θ

board.text: Sine is largest at 90 degrees, so 2θ = 90 and θ = 45 degrees.

questions.q: A ball thrown at 30 degrees and one thrown at 60 degrees, same speed. How do their ranges compare?
options: They land in the same place
questions.why: sin 2θ gives sin 60 for both, because sin 60 = sin 120. Same range, different flight time.

questions.q: You double the launch speed. What happens to the range?
options: It goes up by about 40 percent
questions.why: Range depends on v squared, so doubling the speed multiplies the range by four.

questions.q: Which quantity is unchanged throughout the flight?
questions.why: Nothing acts horizontally, so that component of velocity never changes.

summary: We split projectile motion into independent horizontal and vertical parts, got the time of flight from the vertical alone, computed a real trajectory, and found that 45 degrees maximises range with complementary angles landing together.
